summary:
MODIS and VIIRS both record active-fire hotspots from space, but VIIRS has much finer pixels and reports far more burning in the same place, so the two records cannot be compared directly. FireSync is a web application that harmonizes them so the sensor of origin no longer matters. It snaps both records to a shared 1 km grid, learns a season- and region-specific conversion from the 13 years when both sensors flew together, and produces a single weekly record from 2003 to 2025. From that record it builds a burning-activity calendar for every province and district of Pakistan, showing which periods of the year and which years burn most, and an early-warning view that ranks the current weeks against the same weeks in other years. A user can select a region or a latitude/longitude box and a date range, and download the analytics as CSV. In a blind test, FireSync cuts the error of estimating the VIIRS record from MODIS from 74% to 19%, and its alerts are followed by above-normal burning three times more often than chance. The combined record also shows that Pakistan's autumn burning now arrives about eight days earlier per decade. It matters because crop-residue burning drives
the autumn smog over Punjab, and responders and land managers need a consistent long record to tell an unusual season from a normal one.
details:
FireSync is an interactive web application that harmonizes NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire detections into a consistent 23-year burning record (2003–2025) for Pakistan's provinces and districts.

How it works: FireSync filters low-confidence and non-vegetation detections, converts both sensors into a common 1 km grid using fire cell-days, and applies district- and month-specific calibration factors derived from their 2013–2025 overlap. This eliminates sensor-related inconsistencies and creates a unified historical record.

The application offers seven views: Burning Calendar, Early Warning, This Week, Trends, Harmonization, Map, and Method & Data. Users can explore historical burning patterns, identify unusual fire activity, monitor near-real-time detections, analyze seasonal trends, compare sensor records, search specific regions, and download CSV reports.

Key findings: VIIRS detects 3.9 times more burning than MODIS on the same grid. FireSync reduces blind-test estimation error from 74% to 19% (R² = 0.95). Findings reveal three major burning windows, with Punjab accounting for 70% of detected burning. Burning has increased by 23% per decade, while autumn burning is arriving approximately 8 days earlier per decade. Early-warning alerts were followed by above-normal burning 42% of the time, compared with 9% after normal periods.

Benefits and intended impact: FireSync provides emergency responders, environmental agencies, air-quality forecasters, agricultural extension services, and land managers with a reliable historical baseline to identify unusual burning, anticipate seasonal fire activity, and target high-risk districts before their burning windows open. It aims to support better agricultural planning, fire monitoring, and early intervention, particularly against crop-residue burning and its contribution to Punjab's autumn smog.

Tools and technologies: Python, Pandas, NumPy, Shapely, Plotly, Streamlit, pytest, and NASA FIRMS satellite datasets (MODIS and VIIRS).

Creativity and innovation: FireSync addresses a critical satellite-data continuity problem by introducing district- and month-specific sensor harmonization rather than applying one correction factor nationwide. Its combination of historical climatology, statistical anomaly detection, near-real-time monitoring, trend analysis, and alert backtesting transforms fragmented satellite observations into actionable information.

Factors considered and limitations: The project considers differences in sensor resolution, geographic variation, seasonal burning patterns, detection confidence, missing observations, and data continuity. Fire cell-days measure detected activity rather than actual burned area. Clouds and satellite overpass gaps can hide fires, and alerts indicate statistical anomalies rather than predict fire spread. The current implementation covers Pakistan, with regional searches operating at approximately 11 km resolution.
